skyline.text: Why development economics searches only where the light is
A Bangalore factory shows India’s firms can reach the frontier
What Shah and Kelkar wrote with one reader in mind

footnote.text: Everything the state does has a cost.

brief.head: No rich autocracies
brief.text: Not one advanced economy is an authoritarian country, Ajay Shah said. Rich nations share a package: free speech, rule of law, great firms and falling religiosity. {057-C05}

brief.head: Pray for no windfall
brief.text: Ajay Shah prays that no windfall is ever found under the ground in India. A windfall brings wealth, he said, but not development, and not flourishing people. {057-C06}

brief.head: Fix the mosquitoes
brief.text: Development people confused public health with health care, Ajay Shah said. The state should fix water, sanitation, air and mosquitoes, not build a hospital in every village. {057-C14}

brief.head: Two halves, no talk
brief.text: Boys and girls in India don’t know how to talk to each other, Ajay Shah said. “Just imagine what a schism in the heart of the country.” {057-C09}

brief.head: Clad the reactor
brief.text: Coercive power is poison, Ajay Shah said, and must be clad like a nuclear reactor. Every new power given to the state needs matching cladding. {057-C15}

thought.text: Intentions aren’t enough. Outcomes really matter if you want to make a difference.
thought.who: Amit Varma, closing the episode with a plea to judge policies by results

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the tenfold gap
lead.head: Mind the tenfold gap
body: Why is the average Indian’s output one-tenth of the average American’s, even after adjusting for purchasing power? That, Ajay Shah said, is the single defining question of development economics. {057-C01}
“It’s not 10 percent, it’s not 20 percent,” he said of the gap. “Ten X is a lot.”
The hosts recorded the episode on a mountaintop, with paragliders leaping off nearby and, Shah joked, a hair light 150 million kilometres behind him: the sun.
Amit Varma asked for a sky-high view of the field. This was not about fiscal deficits and inflation, he said, but “real lives, real people. This shit matters.”
## Wrong model, wrong mood

Post-war thinking, Shah said, drew its theory of development from Robert Solow’s growth model, in which output per person depends on capital per person and on productivity, then understood as machines and manuals.
So poor countries were told to save, build up capital and import technology. Development seemed as inevitable as a puppy growing into a dog. Foreign aid would merely speed it up.

India, Shah argued, refutes the model. Only about a third of working-age Indians are employed. Trillions of dollars sit in the global capital market. An English-speaking elite can read any manual. If the model were right, India would already be rich. {#richnow}
The wider record is worse. Of the countries that were poor in 1945, he said, only South Korea, Taiwan, Israel and Chile have become rich. More than a hundred have not.
“So in fact failure is the norm,” Shah said. “Success is the exception.” {057-C04}
Tell a climber that Everest needs only protein bars, he said, and he will approach it differently from one who is told the odds are against him.
## Fix the middle

The data point one way. Lant Pritchett, the hosts’ friend, has found that median income alone explains 99 per cent of the variation in poverty rates across countries. Inequality, welfare programmes and redistribution add up to about 1 per cent.
“Ninety nine percent of the variance of the poverty rate is explained by growth,” Shah said, “not by the obsessions of people who are taking interest in poverty directly.” {057-C07}

Shah’s agenda has three pillars: firms as capable as America’s, a capable state, and a political system in which the state is the agent of the people. The rule of law, he said, is the raw material for the last two.

Behind all three stands society. In the World Values Survey, he said, 50 to 90 per cent of people in advanced economies believe people can generally be trusted; in India the figure is about 15 per cent.
## Under the lamppost

Why did the field lose its way? Shah blamed three incentives: philanthropies hungry for credit, populist politics that rewards handouts, and economics journals that prize rigour over important questions. {057-C17}
Varma, borrowing Pritchett’s frame, called the result kinky development: like a drunk searching for his keys under a lamppost because that is where the light is.
The cure, for Shah, starts in the mind. The dream of the book he wrote with Vijay Kelkar, he said, is that “the journey to development is first and foremost a journey of ideas”.
Varma ended with a plea to think independently and to judge policies by their outcomes, not their intentions, the hosts’ own arguments included.

second.label: Women and freedom
second.head: Breaking up, moving up
second.deck: Amit Varma recalls a column that drew heat, and what divorce rates reveal
body: When Ajay Shah suggested that a good indicator of social progress is the rate of single mothers, Amit Varma offered one of his own. It had once got him a lot of heat.

In a controversial column, Varma had written that one of the great indicators of women’s empowerment in India is a rising divorce rate. More divorces, he said, mean women are being empowered to walk out of bad marriages. “Mostly that’s what it is.” {057-S08}

Shah’s other example was gay marriage, all over the advanced world, he said. For Varma, an advanced economy is a full package of freedom, not only a flourishing marketplace: “freedom of the mind”, “freedom in the bedroom”, “freedom in the public square”. {#freedom}

quote.text: I think the rising divorce rate is fantastic because it means women are being empowered to walk out of bad marriages.

second.caption: the divorce-rate column

third.head: Not for want of a manual
body: On the ride up the mountain, Ajay Shah put a blunt question to Amit Varma. Was their own show, shot by Nomsita and Vaishnav on Sony equipment, inferior in any obvious way to the global state of the art?
Varma saw no important aspect of their production values that fell short. Their microphone, Shah reported him saying, was literally the global state of the art, with little left to improve. {#mic}

For Shah, that was the whole problem in miniature. “We are bright enough to read these manuals,” he said. “We use these capabilities to the hilt, then you’re at the global frontier. So then what went wrong?” {057-S04}
A technology gap, he argued, cannot explain a tenfold gap in incomes. The answer has to lie elsewhere.
third.caption: a show at the global frontier

p2.title: The long climb
p2.deck: From the Solow model to the lamppost: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma retrace the field, chapter by chapter

sections.label: The question
sections.head: Filthy lucre matters
sections.caption: the cost of being poor
body: Development economics, Ajay Shah said, begins with one question: why is India’s per capita GDP, adjusted for purchasing power, one-tenth of America’s? Most countries are poor, so India is only the guiding example. {057-C01}
The economist Robert Lucas, in what Shah called “a beautiful paper” from 1988, wrote that once you start thinking about this question, it is hard to think about anything else. {057-R11}

Shah expected the charge of reductionism: is filthy lucre all that matters? At Indian levels of income, he said, it is “an absolute crisis”. Children are stunted for want of protein. In the North Indian winter, many cannot afford a hot water bath. “I know how miserable I get if I am told not to get a hot water bath,” he said.
## A luxury belief

Amit Varma went further. The idea that money isn’t everything, he said, is a luxury belief, one that elites hold in air-conditioned rooms and feel virtuous about while it hurts the poor. When one medical emergency can destroy you, money is no side issue. {057-C02}

~ Prosperity, for Shah, is about having choices. After Varma’s episode on cycling, he said, he “only walked away with envy at the advanced commercial and organisational culture of Europe”. {057-S09} What people then do with their choices is their birthright.

quote.text: Money is a big freaking deal. The GDP number is a big freaking deal.

sections.label: The old theory
sections.head: The capital mistake
sections.caption: the Solow model
body: Post-war development thinking, Ajay Shah said, grew out of the growth model of Robert Solow, the MIT economist and Nobel laureate. Output per person depended on capital per person and on productivity, which was thought of as machines. Hidden inside, he said, was a theory of development. {057-J09}

The prescription followed: save, build up capital, buy the right machines, read the right manuals. The shortage was real. Before he first went abroad for his PhD, Shah said, he had never seen a highway in India. {057-S01}
## Secret runes

UN bodies, UNIDO or UNCTAD, he could not remember which, obsessed over “technology transfer”, as if rich countries guarded secret runes. His father told him this was completely wrong. The knowledge was in books, papers, manuals and patents, and “the burden is on us”. {057-S02}
Shah’s verdict on the old model was blunt. “The idea that productivity is a manual, a document that can be transmitted beggars the imagination,” he said. {057-C03}
~ The old model assumed that India’s plentiful English speakers would bring the manuals in, and that would be that. “We are all Macaulay’s children,” Shah said. {057-J12}

quote.text: All the knowledge is there in the books, it’s there in the papers, you buy the machine, you get the manual

sections.label: The record
sections.head: Not a puppy, a mountain
sections.caption: why failure is the norm
body: In the dawn of development there was a lot of optimism, Ajay Shah said. The very word suggested a child growing into an adult, or a puppy into a dog: inevitable, needing only calories and protein. Foreign aid and technology transfer were the nutrients.
Amit Varma, the philosopher of the pair, objected that a puppy growing into a dog is “actually deeply tragic”. {057-J02}
The optimists were wrong. Of the countries that were poor in 1945, Shah said, only four have become rich: South Korea, Taiwan, Israel and Chile. {#four}
## Respect the ladder

More than a hundred did not, and in 2024, he said, nobody can say “just hang in there” any more. Failure is the norm. Yet the development community, he thought, still runs on “too much optimism”, the better to drum up money from donors. {057-C04}

His metaphor was Everest. Tell a climber it is just a matter of eating enough protein bars, and he will approach it differently. Tell him there is a high chance he will not make it, and he will train.
~ Varma called it a brilliant metaphor. Climbing Everest is possible, he said, and so is becoming a developed country, with the right approach.

quote.text: We will all do better by respecting the ladder that we seek to climb.

sections.label: The first pillar
sections.head: Where GDP is made
sections.caption: the firm as the engine of growth
body: Output is made in firms, Ajay Shah said, and that is the first grand pillar of development economics. Firms turn people, capital, machines, manuals and patents into output, and there is real magic in that. “If it was simple, it would have happened by now.” {057-C10}

What makes the United States great, he had said earlier, is not its government but Google, Microsoft and JP Morgan. He urged readers not just to shop at IKEA but to walk around it and admire the “audacity of conception”. {057-R21}

Yet development economics neglects firms, Shah said, because they are seen as rich people that funders and journals don’t care for. Studying them would reveal the policy failures that hold them back. Firms and finance, he said, are how India got to a three trillion dollar GDP. {#trillion}
## Seen and unseen

Amit Varma saw a classic case of the seen and the unseen. What is seen is what firms have achieved; what is unseen is what bad laws stopped them achieving. Labour laws with the best of intentions, he said, cripple the growth of firms and so hurt workers. Everything the state does has a cost.
~ Varma also rejected the trio of state, society and market. There are only two, he said: markets are just how members of society do things for one another, voluntarily. {057-C11}

quote.text: The first grand pillar of development economics is this cold statement that output is made in firms.

sections.label: The state
sections.head: Growth flatters the state
sections.caption: why growth can hide a failing state
body: Economic growth does not mean the state got better, Ajay Shah warned, though many Indians assume it must have. Development comes in spurts, and in a spurt the two can run in contrary directions. {057-C12}

The book *Building State Capability*, by Matt Andrews, Lant Pritchett and co-authors, measured it carefully, he said, and found that Indian state capability got worse during the 1991-2011 boom. {057-R12}

Shah offered a conjecture. As the economy grows, bigger sums are waved before the same judges, regulators and officials, and checks built for a smaller economy break down. Good growth numbers breed complacency, so the energy to criticise the government fades. Growth episodes, he said, contain the seeds of their own fall.
Amit Varma added that money flowing in turns the state into a beast that feeds itself and gets bloated.
## The hare and the tortoise

The UK and the US, Shah said, grew at 3 per cent for 200 years and never faltered. {#threepercent} Developing economies, by contrast, have been more of a hare than a tortoise, growing in spurts. {#hare}

~ Shah cited a line he called beautiful, from John Maynard Keynes: the state’s job is not to do things a little better than private people, but to do what the private sector will not do at all. {057-J17}

quote.text: So we should not make the mistake of jumping to the conclusion that because GDP growth happened, state capability got better.

sections.label: The distortion
sections.head: Bright light, wrong place
sections.caption: the drunk and the lamppost
body: One frame from Lant Pritchett, Amit Varma said, made him see more clearly and also made him angry: national development versus kinky development. National development raises median income, which is what gets people out of poverty. Kinky development zooms in on a narrow problem that can be solved and claimed.

Varma’s picture was a drunk searching under a lamppost, helped by a polite Mumbai cop. Where did he drop his keys? A hundred metres away, in the dark bushes. Then why look here? “Because the light is here.” {057-J20}
Mainstream development economics does the same, Varma said, with RCTs on ridiculously trivial questions, such as whether treated mosquito nets help with malaria: easy wins for careers. {057-C16}
## Three incentives

Ajay Shah blamed incentives. Philanthropists may be noble, but their staff need wins to claim, and consultants end up doing a joint secretary’s office work. He imagined the boast: “I contributed to this policy that got 73.4 people out of poverty.” {057-J06}
Populist politics prefers saying “I gave you 2000 rupees” to creating conditions for growth, he said. {#rupees}
~ And in “the peculiar frat boy world of the economics journals”, referees ask for twenty changes and prize rigour over important questions. {057-J07}

quote.text: I feel that the entire field of mainstream development economics is doing that. They are searching for easy answers that don’t matter.

side.boxText: Amit Varma wished that Lant Pritchett’s “disembodied spirit” from the future had sat in Nehru’s cabinet meetings. Pritchett’s data, that median income explains 99 per cent of poverty rates, anchors the episode. Ajay Shah calls it “a very important story”. {057-R02}

contQuote.text: Look around us in India today. Most people continue to have a big state delusion. You go to the average private business person, how will you fix the country? They want government to do more, not less.

p3.title: Tales from the mountain
p3.deck: Four stories from the climb, and what each says about development

stories.start: And I just want to dwell on like Taiwan, Israel, Korea.
stories.end: under very adverse circumstances did manage to claw their way out of it.
stories.caption: the terrible starts of three success stories
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Taiwan, Korea and Israel
stories.head: Bad beginnings, rich endings
body: Since 1945, only four poor countries have become rich: South Korea, Taiwan, Israel and Chile. Amit Varma called that “such a sobering and cautionary tale”, but also inspiring: if they can do it, he said, so can we.
Ajay Shah wanted to dwell on how three of them began. “What a terrible beginning for each of them,” he said.

Taiwan, he said, was an irrelevant island off the coast of China that had endured a very cruel Japanese occupation. After the Chinese communist revolution, people fleeing the mainland poured in. Their leader, Chiang Kai-shek, was no great person. “He’s no Nehru,” Shah said. “He’s a pretty rotten person in his own ways.”

Then Korea. The line between North and South runs essentially at Seoul, and during the Korean War the city was taken and retaken six times. {#seoul} With Second World War equipment, Shah said, Seoul should be thought of as destroyed on the scale of Berlin, Stalingrad or Dresden.
There are stories, he added, of early South Korean government officials looking up to India and trying to learn from its civil service practices.

And Israel. It fought a war in 1948, every step was a struggle, and it was surrounded by hostile states. “If you think fighting a two-front war is difficult, think of what Israel has been through,” Shah said.
~ Yet some countries placed under very adverse circumstances, he said, did manage to claw their way out. {057-S05}

quote.text: So these things are very hard and they can be done.

stories.start: we talked about my uh happiest moment of recent months.
stories.end: read the manuals, deploy them into India. There is no technical barrier.
stories.caption: the blue jeans factory
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s happiest moment of recent months
stories.head: Denim at the cutting edge
body: One of Ajay Shah’s happiest moments in recent months was a visit to a blue jeans factory on the outskirts of Bangalore. {057-S03}

The people running it, he said, are in touch with the global state of the art. They know every machine available anywhere. They carefully work out the return on each one and decide which machine to adopt when.
Then they go to China, to Taiwan or to Europe, buy the machines, read the manuals and deploy them in India. “There is no technical barrier,” Shah said.

~ That was the puzzle. Labour is plentiful, capital in the world market is “infinite”, and the manuals are readable. If the old Solow model were true, Shah said, “by now India should have been a rich country”.
stories.why: Knowledge is not what India lacks: its best firms can already buy and run the world’s best machines. Meanwhile about two-thirds of working-age Indians are not working, Shah said, and that is what development must explain. {#employment}

stories.start: So for me personally in my life journey It has been a huge experience
stories.end: the fashion of the times would indicate that we need a big state.
stories.caption: the book for Nehru
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah and Vijay Kelkar’s private brief
stories.head: A book for Nehru’s time machine
body: Economists, Ajay Shah said, are raised on the Solow model: pile on capital, bring in machines and manuals, and development should follow. Stepping out of it took him a very long time.
Slowly he came to state capability, the rule of law, checks and balances and public choice theory, “the central engine of thinking about the misbehaviour of the state”.

He and Vijay Kelkar had worked in the Ministry of Finance. Writing *In Service of the Republic*, their private brief was a question: which one book would they send in a time machine to Jawaharlal Nehru? {057-S07}

~ Amit Varma spelt out the assumption: Nehru was a man of high intellect and great intentions. But public choice theory did not exist, Varma said, and Hayek was not taken that seriously, even though *The Road to Serfdom* was a bestseller.
stories.why: Policy failure often reflects the ideas available at the time rather than bad intentions. That is why Shah calls the journey to development “first and foremost a journey of ideas”. {057-C13}

stories.start: And also if we go d deeper into the minds of those people,
stories.end: So Nehruvian high modernism is alive and well in the country, even today.
stories.caption: the world of 1947
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah reconstructs the mood of 1947
stories.head: All the world’s a war economy
body: To explain India’s choice of a big state, Ajay Shah went into the minds of its founders, who weighed a UK-type strategy against a USSR-type one.

Russia had lost a war to Japan in 1905 and been whipped at Tannenberg in 1916, Shah said. {#tannenberg} Then the communists kicked in the door, and a civil war ran till 1921. By 1945 it was the greatest land power in the world.

By the end of the Second World War, every major combatant ran a commanded economy, to varying extents: the USSR; Germany, where private firms worked at the Nazis’ call; a UK war economy managed largely by John Maynard Keynes; and a US that passed a law to give orders to private firms.
~ Standing in 1945, Shah said, the illusion of the state on top was easy to slip into. {057-S06}

quote.text: So it was very easy to slip into a state on top illusion.

quiz.q: Of the countries poor in 1945, which four does Ajay Shah say have since become rich?
quiz.a: South Korea, Taiwan, Israel and Chile; more than a hundred others have not.

quiz.q: What share of cross-country variation in poverty rates does median income explain, in Lant Pritchett’s finding?
quiz.a: Ninety-nine per cent; inequality, welfare and redistribution add up to about one per cent.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah’s father say about the old UN fixation on technology transfer?
quiz.a: That it was wrong: the knowledge is all in books, papers, manuals and patents.

quiz.q: Besides shopping there, what does Ajay Shah urge readers to do at IKEA?
quiz.a: Walk around and admire the company: its design, manufacturing, stores and marketing.

quiz.q: Why did Amit Varma once argue that a rising divorce rate is good news?
quiz.a: It means women are being empowered to walk out of bad marriages.

quiz.q: In Keynes’s line quoted by Shah, what is the job of the state?
quiz.a: To do the things the private sector will not do at all.
